blocks.text: On the word צפור tsippor, which denotes both birds of any kind and specifically the sparrow. Its kinds according to the Arabs; and on the house sparrow and its chirping.

Among the infirmities of old age which Solomon vividly depicts, this too is listed, Eccles. XII, 6.: that one is roused and rises לקול הצפור, at the voice of the tsippor, or bird, that is, of the cock, as many think. The most learned Mercerus refutes them thus: Those who understand the cock, at whose voice one is roused, do not understand the force of the Hebrew word צפור (tsippor), which means a little bird, etc., and is not said of larger birds. And the same author in his Thesaurus: צפור (tsippor) means smaller birds, etc.; עוף (oph), however, is a bird or winged creature in general. And Schindler: צפור (tsippor) is a little bird flying about, or one that circles in the air. It comprises the smaller birds, and among them the sparrow, the one most frequently found among men, a very common bird. So too most other recent lexicographers. And in Philo's book Who is the Heir of Divine Things, Sepphora is ὀρνίθιον [ornithion], a little bird. Yet among the Hebrews עוף oph and צפור tsippor are equally general, and both names embrace absolutely all winged creatures. Hence Kimchi and Pomarius in their Lexicons, under the word צפור tsippor: שם כלל לכל עוף, it is a name common to every bird. And Aquinas: שם כולל לכל מיני עוף שיעופף, This name comprises every species of bird that flies. That this is entirely true will be clear to anyone who compares the passages of Scripture. For in Deut. IV, 17., when God forbids the worship of תבנית כל צפור כנף אשר תעוף בשמים, the likeness of any winged tsippor that flies through the heavens, who would say that only the worship of little birds is forbidden, and not that of larger birds as well? And in Deut. XIV, 11., when the same God permits the eating of כל צפור טהורה, every clean tsippor, will he be said to have permitted only little birds, and not hens, guinea fowl and pheasants? Or who ever restricted to little birds the law found in Deut. XXII, 6.: If there come before you קן צפור, a nest of a tsippor, in any tree or on the ground, a nest of young or of eggs, where the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, do not take the mother with the young? Again, who would deny that all birds are meant when we read that God subjected to man the beasts of the field, צפור שמים, the tsippor of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, Psal. VIII, 9.? Or when [col. 146] wild beasts, and all cattle, creeping things, וצפור כנף, and the winged tsippor are invited to praise God, Psal. CXLVIII, 10.? Or when we read that in the branches of the mystical tree dwell כל צפור כל כנף, every tsippor, everything winged, Ezech. XVII, 23.? And in the plural, צפרי שמיא, the tsippare of the heavens, Dan. IV, 9. 18.? Finally, it is clear that birds of prey, which are generally by far the largest, are designated by this name, when in Ezech. XXXIX, 4. 17. God hands over the hosts of Gog and Magog to be devoured לעיט צפור, [II, 722] by the ravenous winged tsippor. And in Daniel IV, 20, where the nails of the Babylonian king are said to have grown כצפרין, like tsipparin, that is, like the talons of birds of prey, which from the curvature and size of their talons are called in Greek γαμψώνυχες [gampsōnyches]. It is therefore evident that the name צפור tsippor extends even to the largest birds. Rabbi Moses, son of Gershom, maintains that birds are so called שבעלות השחר מתחילות לרנן ולצפצוף, because at the rising of the dawn they begin to sing and to warble. I, for my part, hold that they are named not from singing, which is not common to all, but from צפר, that is, morning; because it is customary for birds to rise very early in the morning, whether they are songbirds or not, while wild beasts are then sound asleep, because they spend the night awake, Psal. CIV, 20.
